role: Part A runner: 24 processes of bw_old and bw_new with 120 threads.
purpose: `ra.sh` repeats the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13 with the binaries `bw_old` and `bw_new` of that day: 24 processes, one per binary, kernel and round, each with 120 threads on CPUs 0 to 119. It builds nothing, and it writes the rows that the binaries print to `threads120.csv` and the machine state to `probe.txt` in a new result folder.

main_flow.step: Set the shell options that stop the script at a failed command and at an unset variable. Then restart the script under `taskset -c 0-119`. The script and every process that it starts may then use CPUs 0 to 119 only.
Read the argument `NAME` (`T72A1`, `T72A2` or `T72A3` in go.sh). Stop if the marker file exists.
Compare the sha256 of `bw_old` and `bw_new` with the values of 2026-11-13. Stop on a difference.
Create the result folder `k120-NAME-TIME` (`TIME` is the UTC time).
Wait until at most 2 tasks are runnable (at most 40 readings, 1 s apart), then 5 s more. Stop if more than 2 tasks stay runnable. After the wait, check the marker file again.
Write host, time, load averages, boot id, `MemTotal`, Linux kernel release, the 5 processes with the highest %CPU and the checksums to `probe.txt`.
Round 1, 12 processes: for each kernel in the order `read`, `write`, `copy`, `asmread`, `asmwrite`, `asmcopy`, first `bw_old`, then `bw_new`. Each process appends its rows to `threads120.csv`.
Round 2, 12 processes: the same processes in the exact reverse order. The last two are `bw_new` with `read`, then `bw_old` with `read`.
Append the load averages after the last process to `probe.txt` and print the result folder.

behavior_notes: Nothing in this script runs inside a timed interval. The script starts a binary and waits for it. The clock reads, the pinning of the threads and the buffers are in the binary [Ref2].

What one process does with its arguments [Ref2]: each of the 120 threads first pins itself to one CPU (thread number i to CPU i). Then it allocates its own buffer of 256 MiB and asks Linux for huge pages for it (`madvise` with `MADV_HUGEPAGE`). Then it writes its whole buffer once before any timing (first touch). It writes with `k_write`, the function of the kernel `write` of the same binary. For `copy` and `asmcopy` each thread has a second buffer of the same size.

Timing inside one process [Ref2]: before each of the 3 intervals every thread runs the kernel once over its buffer without timing. Then all threads start together. A thread reads the clock at its start and after each whole pass over its buffer. It stops when 0.5 s or more have passed. So the threads stop at different times (whole-pass stop).

The rate [Ref2]: the binary prints one row per interval. For `read` and `asmread` a thread counts 268435456 bytes per pass over its buffer. It counts the same number for `write` and `asmwrite`. For `copy` and `asmcopy` it counts twice that number: the bytes that it read plus the bytes that it wrote. The column `aggregate_GBps` is the sum of the bytes of all threads, divided by the longest elapsed time of any thread, in GB/s. Each process also prints a comment line, a title line and one `best` row with the highest of its 3 rates.

Machine code of the two read kernels, from the listing of 2026-11-13 [Ref1]: one loop pass of the old read kernel in `bw_old` has 4 `ldp q` loads (128 bytes) and 8 vector `add` instructions that add the loaded values to the running sums. One loop pass of the new read kernel in `bw_new` has 8 `ldp q` loads (256 bytes) and no instruction that uses the loaded values. The listing agrees with the comment on lines 4 and 5 of ra.sh: 8 vector registers hold the 16 running sums of the old read kernel, and the new read kernel has loads only.

Order of the processes: one process holds one kernel of one binary. So no kernel is timed after another kernel in the same process. But the processes follow each other without a wait. In round 1 the old read kernel is process 1 and the new read kernel is process 2. In round 2 the new read kernel is process 23 and the old read kernel is process 24.

The wait of lines 26 to 28 uses the number of tasks that are runnable at that moment. It does not use the load average. In sessions 2 and 3 the 1-minute load average after the wait was 98.64 and 102.96, and `probe.txt` records `runnable=2` [Ref3].

The 1-minute load average is higher at the last process of a session than at the first process. The line that starts with `-- ` records it at the start of each process. It was 0.07 for process 1 and 77.06 for process 24 in session 1, 98.64 and 112.71 in session 2, and 102.96 and 111.98 in session 3 [Ref3]. It does not rise at every process. In session 3 it fell from 105.51 at process 5 to 98.02 at process 6 [Ref3].

The marker file is checked before each process and not while a process runs. In the three sessions the start of a process came 2 s to 5 s after the start of the process before it [Ref3]. These start times have a resolution of 1 s. rx.sh checks the file every second while a process runs. When the file exists, rx.sh stops that process [Ref5].

The script can stop early. Status 1: no `NAME`. Status 2: a binary is not the one of 2026-11-13, or cannot be read. Status 3: the marker file exists. Status 6: more than 2 tasks are runnable after 40 readings. A benchmark process that fails stops the script with its own status. go.sh stops the whole run when ra.sh ends with a status other than 0 [Ref4].

The main differences between ra.sh and the 120-thread part of run_kernels.sh: ra.sh builds nothing and runs no self-test. It checks the checksums of the binaries. It waits before the first process, and it runs no one-thread process before the 120-thread processes. It records the boot id, `MemTotal`, the Linux kernel release and the runnable tasks. It does not record the gcc version and the compiler flags. The function `one`, the two kernel lists and the loop have the same text in both scripts [Ref7].
The local file is the script that ran. Its sha256 (6d67715e...) equals the value that `probe.txt` records in all three sessions [Ref3].

The records show two texts of the new source `bandwidth.c`. The local file has the sha256 f1985072... [Ref2]. The timed run of 2026-11-13 recorded the sha256 c1406e02... for `bandwidth.c` in its `probe.txt` [Ref1]. All three `probe.txt` files that run_kernels.sh wrote on that day record the same sha256 for `bw_new` (fd7c14df...) [Ref1] [Ref9]. ra.sh checks this value. So the machine code is not in doubt. The two texts differ in comment lines only. An edit of 2026-11-13 18:32:07 UTC replaced 2 comment lines above `k_read` with the 5 comment lines 178 to 182 of the local text [Ref11]. With this edit reversed, the local text has the sha256 value of the earlier text (c1406e02...). No code line differs.
The binaries `bw_old` and `bw_new` are not in the local folders. Their sha256 values are known only from records such as lines 17 and 18 of ra.sh and the `probe.txt` files [Ref1] [Ref3] [Ref9].

words.def: the Arm reference server under test. It has 128 CPUs.
the two halves of the chip. CPUs 0-63 sit on mesh 0. CPUs 64-127 sit on mesh 1.
our runs use CPUs 0-119 only: 64 threads on mesh 0 plus 56 threads on mesh 1. Each thread reads its own buffer of 256 MiB from memory.
the inner loop of the benchmark that reads memory. On this page "kernel" means this loop. The operating system kernel is always written "Linux kernel".
portable C code with 16 running sums. Each load is followed by an add. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_old and `oldread` in the runner bwx12.
NEON intrinsics (C functions that map to Arm vector instructions), loads only. Its name is `read` in the binary bw_new and `read` in bwx12.
a hand-written load-only loop. It has the same 8 "ldp q" loads per 256 B as the new read kernel. "ldp q" is the Arm instruction that loads two 16-byte vector registers.
the instructions that the compiler produced for a function. The listing is their text form. run_kernels.sh wrote it to its own `probe.txt` on 2026-11-13 [Ref1].
one execution of the body of a loop.

the four other kernels of bw_old and bw_new. `write` fills a buffer. `copy` copies one buffer to a second buffer. `asmwrite` and `asmcopy` are hand-written loops for the same two jobs. They are not read kernels.
the benchmark and its two binaries of 2026-11-13. bw_old was built from the old source, bw_new from the new source.
later runner programs for the same loops. They print one row per thread. bwx12 is the runner of the 2026-11-15 investigation. bwx11 and bwx are older versions.
test loops of bwx12: the asmread loop with 96 or 256 no-operation instructions per 256 B, and a loop with one load per 64 B line.

a process is one start of a benchmark binary. An interval is one timed measurement inside a process. bwx12 times a sequence of kernels and repeats the sequence: each repeat is a round (counted from 0), and the position is the place of a kernel in the sequence (counted from 0). In part A the round (1 or 2) is the round of the script: round 2 runs the processes in the reverse order.
one pass of go.sh through part A, part L and part C.
the 120-thread part of the test of 2026-11-13, repeated with the same two binaries.
one bwx12 process with the kernel sequence oldread, asmread, read_nop96, read_nop256, read_1pl.
one bwx12 process with the sequence oldread, read, asmread (cfwd) or asmread, read, oldread (crev).
the driver script of the rerun of 2026-11-17. It calls ra.sh once per session.
the script of 2026-11-13. It built bw_old and bw_new and ran the test for the first time.
the GNU C compiler. run_kernels.sh built bw_old and bw_new with it [Ref7].
the program `selftest`. run_kernels.sh builds it and runs it before its timed processes [Ref7]. It checks what the kernels of the new source do to memory [Ref10].
the script that starts the bwx12 processes of part L and part C.
an analysis script that reads threads120.csv.
`/tmp/positron-perf.RUNNING`. Another user creates it during a performance test [Ref8]. Our scripts stop when it exists.

the number of tasks that are runnable or wait for disk input and output, averaged by Linux over the last 1, 5 and 15 minutes (file /proc/loadavg). The fourth field of the file gives the tasks that are runnable now and the number of all tasks.

the column pcpu of the tool ps. It is the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started. So it is an average over the life of the process. It is not the use at the moment of the reading.
a random identifier that Linux creates at each start. Equal boot ids mean the same boot.
the usable memory that Linux reports, in kB.
a checksum. Two files with the same sha256 have the same content.
the stop rule of bandwidth.c: after the minimum time (0.5 s here) each thread finishes the pass over its buffer that it is in. The threads stop at different times.
memory pages of 2 MiB that Linux can use for a buffer in place of its smaller standard pages.
the first write of a thread to its new buffer. The benchmark does it before any timing, so that a timed interval holds no page fault.
a thread that is pinned to a CPU may run on that CPU only.
GB = 1e9 bytes. MiB = 2^20 bytes. The argument `256M` means 256 MiB = 268435456 bytes.
the number that a program returns when it ends. 0 means success.
Coordinated Universal Time. The scripts write every time in UTC.
a Linux tool that starts a command with a limit on the CPUs that the command may use.
